entities.summary:
Herculaneum, located near modern-day Ercolano, Italy, was an ancient Roman town established in the 6th century BCE, particularly renowned for its remarkable preservation due to the catastrophic eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 CE. This archaeological site, alongside Pompeii, provides invaluable insights into Roman life, architecture, and urban planning, reflecting the cultural and social dynamics of the time. Its discovery in the 18th century catalyzed a renewed interest in classical antiquity and has influenced historical methodologies, notably in archaeology and art history.

The excavation of Herculaneum revealed well-preserved structures, including the Villa of the Papyri, which housed a significant library of philosophical texts, illustrating the intellectual pursuits of the elite class during the Roman Empire. The town was buried under approximately 20 meters of volcanic material, which protected many artifacts from deterioration, allowing historians to reconstruct daily life in a Roman city. The site featured advanced engineering, such as an intricate drainage system, and decorative frescoes that showcase the artistic achievements of the era.

Herculaneum's legacy extends beyond its archaeological significance; it has shaped modern understanding of the Roman world, influencing art, literature, and historical narratives. The texts recovered from the Villa of the Papyri have contributed to the study of Epicurean philosophy, impacting Western thought. Moreover, the site has inspired countless artists and writers throughout history, serving as a poignant reminder of the fragility of civilization in the face of natural disasters.
